extracted.intended_audience: licensing counsel and patent attorneys negotiating patent licenses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining a reasonable royalty in patent licensing negotiations, covering how to identify and apportion the royalty base and royalty rate, apply Georgia‑Pacific factors and alternative valuation methods, and adjust for negotiation-specific risks (invalidity, non-infringement, business considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a credible patent valuation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensor should use a credible patent valuation methodology during patent license negotiations to obtain optimum returns; for large portfolios valuation may be based on a small set of important patents rather than a statistical portfolio value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuation methodology can be based on a typical reasonable royalty analysis conducted during the damages phase of patent infringement litigation. Important for licensors of large portfolios where evaluating each patent is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie reasonable royalty to claimed invention's marketplace footprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalty determination must be tied to the claimed invention's footprint in the marketplace and is typically determined by a hypothetical negotiation between a willing licensor and willing licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical negotiation is determined at the time just before infringement began and is based on the assumption that the patent is valid and infringed (ResQNet.com; Lucent Technologies). The royalty typically equals a specified royalty rate applied to a royalty base; counsel must ensure the rate and base correspond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze royalty base and rate for each patent-product pair
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel should determine the reasonable royalty base and rate for each patent and product or service pair when licensing a portfolio, because each patent may have different value for different products and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires evidence tending to separate or apportion between patented and unpatented features (LaserDynamics v. Quanta). Perform per-pair analyses rather than blanket portfolio assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (1): Royalties received by the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties received by the patentee for the licensing of the patent in suit tending to show an established royalty rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the 15 Georgia‑Pacific factors courts commonly consider in hypothetical negotiation frameworks (Georgia‑Pacific Corp. v. U.S. Plywood Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (2): Rates paid by the licensee for other patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Rates paid by the licensee for the use of other comparable patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare licensee's prior rates where appropriate and comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (3): Nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature and scope of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider exclusivity, fields of use, territorial scope, and other license scope elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (4): Licensor's policy and marketing program
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensor's established policy and marketing program to maintain patent monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether licensor enforces patents aggressively, pricing/marketing strategies to preserve monopoly value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (5): Commercial relationship between parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial relationship between the licensor and licensee, such as whether they are business competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationship can affect bargaining power and the negotiated rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (6): Effect on sales of non‑patented items
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect or value as a generator of sales of non‑patented items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether patented feature drives sales of complementary or non‑patented products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (7): Duration and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of the patent and term of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer remaining patent life or longer license term can increase royalty value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (8): Profitability and commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Profitability, commercial success, and popularity of products made under patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success evidence can support higher royalties, but must be tied to the patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (9): Utility and advantages over old modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility and advantages of the patent over old modes or devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical and practical advantages versus prior solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (10): Nature, character, and benefits to users
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature, character, and benefits of the patented invention to users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider user value and practical benefits attributable to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (11): Extent of use by infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of use by infringer and evidence probative of the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of adoption/use by infringer supports valuation of the technology's economic footprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (12): Portion of profit customary to allow
rubrics_metrics.description: Portion of profit customary to allow for use of the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry norms and customary profit shares inform reasonable splits between licensor and licensee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (13): Portion of realizable profit to credit to the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Portion of realizable profit that should be credited to the patented invention as distinguished from the business risks or features added by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires apportionment to separate patent contribution from other business features or risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (14): Opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion testimony of qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence is commonly used to support valuation, apportionment, and rate determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors (15): Hypothetical negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical negotiation between licensor and licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overarching construct: courts emulate what parties would have agreed to just before infringement under assumed validity/infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining range and profit‑split approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a bargaining range: maximum equal to expected incremental benefits/profits licensor receives from selling product with the patented feature; minimum equal to licensor's incremental cost from licensing the patented feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximum is found by comparing product with patented feature vs otherwise identical product using next‑best alternative or omitting the feature; minimum is licensor's incremental cost from licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty base principle: apportion to patented feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The royalty base should focus on the product portion attributable to the patented feature, not unpatented features; requires either EMVR or apportionment to smallest saleable patent‑practicing unit (SSU).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider product purpose, the patented feature, importance of the patented feature to product purpose, and the patented feature's advantages over alternatives. Use reliable and tangible evidence; absolute precision not required (VirnetX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: EMVR is a narrow exception allowing the entire product value as royalty base when the patented technology is what motivates consumers to buy the overall product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely being required or important is insufficient; must show patented technology motivates purchase. Preferably components of a multi‑component product work as a single functioning unit (LaserDynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest Saleable Patent‑Practicing Unit (SSU)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: royalties should be based on the SSU to limit compensation for non‑infringing components; counsel must understand claimed invention because it may broadly relate to different potential SSUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EMVR does not apply, identify SSU, then determine whether patented feature has value beyond SSU and apportion accordingly. In negotiation, licensor may propose a larger base if factual support exists that patented feature impacts multiple components (Fractus v. Samsung).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi‑component SSU apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the SSU is a multi‑component product containing non‑infringing features unrelated to the patented feature, the patented feature must be apportioned within the SSU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment helps prevent overcompensation for unrelated features (VirnetX; Mirror Worlds). Use evidence to support the apportionment approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence to support apportionment/value beyond SSU
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual support is required to assert that a patented feature has value beyond the SSU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use industry papers, expert testimony, marketing documents, comparisons with similar products without the patented feature, and other reliable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty rate cap: incremental benefits and bargaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty rate is typically capped by the parties' respective incremental benefits, which depend on their relative bargaining power in a hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bargaining power is determined by Georgia‑Pacific factors and other economic considerations (industry, technology). Courts require credible and reliable evidence supporting the rate's starting point (Uniloc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable license rates method
rubrics_metrics.description: Where adequate comparable rates exist, prior license agreements for the same or similar technology/products can be the basis for the current royalty rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust prior rates for material differences (technology differences, economic circumstances, scope, grantbacks, lump sums, base applied). If adjustments are not possible, exclude the comparable. Example: adjust rate by ratio of original base to apportioned base to derive equivalent rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology‑defined royalty rate
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty rate based on determinable technology quantities: proper apportionment to product, and an industry royalty rate applied uniformly across the apportioned base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determined from technology details, value of the patent to the technology, and industry's valuation of the technology. Advantages: reduces royalty stacking concerns, avoids costly customer polling, fits negotiation settings and portfolio approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other royalty rate methods: next‑best alternative, cost savings, incremental profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have used other techniques such as comparing the patented feature to the next‑best available alternative, quantifying cost savings, and measuring incremental profits from the patented feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Next‑best alternative must include all associated costs, be available at negotiation time, acceptable to consumers, and be supported by reliable evidence (Grain Processing; AFT Trust). Cost savings require dollar‑valued evidence; incremental profits often determined by expert reports or public proxies in negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust comparable rates when base differs (ratio method)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comparable license applied a rate against a different base (e.g., entire product), do not mechanically apply that rate to an apportioned base; instead take the ratio of the comparable license base to the apportioned base and multiply that ratio by the comparable rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a larger rate for the licensor consistent with an apportioned (smaller) base — illustrated with smartphone example converting 0.05% on $640 to ~16% on $2 apportioned base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard‑essential patents (SEPs) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs subject to RAND/FRAND commitments, many Georgia‑Pacific factors may be irrelevant; royalty must be apportioned to the patented invention's incremental value, not value from standardization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on the incremental contribution of the patent to the product, avoiding inflated royalties tied to standardization (Ericsson v. D‑Link).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation‑specific risk discounts (invalidity/non‑infringement/business)
rubrics_metrics.description: In negotiations, the reasonable royalty should be discounted by the risk that the patents are invalid or not infringed and other business considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk expressed between 0% (clear invalidity or missing claim element) and 100% (no possibility of invalidity and all claim elements practiced). Assign risk ranges by understanding potential litigation challenges, file history, and case law. Formula: Reasonable Royalty(Negotiated) = ((Royalty Base) × (Reasonable Royalty Rate)) × Risk of Invalidity × Risk of Non‑infringement × Business Considerations Factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation business considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In negotiation, business factors (litigation cost avoidance, delay to payment, customer relationships, quarterly revenue expectations) should influence the negotiated royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors can justify discounts or adjustments relative to litigation‑style damages calculations that compensate for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public data and internal expertise when experts are infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: In negotiations where surveys and expert witnesses are too costly or time‑consuming, parties may rely on internal expertise and public industry data to estimate incremental profits or other valuation inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of public proxies: market share shifts after feature adoption, price differentials between otherwise identical products with/without feature; exercise caution due to confounding factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio valuation consistency using technology‑defined rates
rubrics_metrics.description: For patent portfolios applied to the same product type, parties may consistently use a technology‑defined royalty rate for each patent if the patent's actual value contribution to the overall product has been determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate when the apportioned royalty base reflects properly apportioned patented feature value across the product type.
